report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. info.title: Same Gossip, Different Judgment: Why Inappropriate Workplace Gossip Is More Acceptable When It Targets AI

text.text: Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming an active member of organizational teams.
Yet successful human-AI symbiosis depends on more than intelligent algorithms, trust calibration, or effective task allocation.
As AI becomes a social interaction partner, organizations must also establish shared moral norms governing how artificial teammates are treated.
Surprisingly, little is known about whether employees apply the same ethical standards to AI coworkers as they do to human colleagues or why these judgments differ.

To address this question, we conducted two preregistered online vignette experiments (N = 546) in which participants observed coworkers engaging in identical inappropriate workplace gossip directed either at a human colleague or an AI teammate.
Building on Bandura's theory of moral disengagement, we tested whether cognitive moral disengagement explains differences in observers' moral evaluations and willingness to intervene.

Across both studies, participants consistently judged gossip about an AI teammate as more morally acceptable and reported significantly lower willingness to intervene than when the same behavior targeted a human colleague.
AI also increased endorsement of all eight mechanisms of moral disengagement.

Parallel mediation analyses showed that moral disengagement fully accounted for the effects of target identity on both outcome variables, indicating that AI changes the cognitive processes through which observers evaluate unethical workplace behavior.
Although the specific mechanisms contributing unique indirect effects varied somewhat across studies, dehumanization and distortion of consequences emerged as the most robust mediators.
An exploratory analysis further demonstrated that these effects generalized across male and female perpetrators.
These findings extend research on human-AI symbiosis by identifying shared moral norms as a previously overlooked prerequisite for successful collaboration.

They suggest that organizations should focus not only on designing trustworthy AI systems but also on fostering ethical workplace cultures in which inappropriate behavior is evaluated according to the behavior itself rather than whether its target is human or artificial.
Imagine overhearing two coworkers ridiculing another member of their team.
They mock poor performance, question competence, and make derogatory remarks behind the person's back.
Most observers would probably consider such behavior inappropriate and expect someone to intervene.
But would the same moral judgment apply if the target were not a human colleague, but an AI teammate?
This omission is particularly striking because organizations are fundamentally social systems.
Their functioning depends not only on formal rules but also on informal norms that define which behaviors are considered acceptable and which are condemned.
These norms emerge through countless everyday interactions in which employees continuously evaluate the behavior of others.
Observers play a particularly important role in this process because they determine whether inappropriate behavior is tolerated, challenged, or sanctioned.
Their reactions influence whether isolated incidents remain exceptions or gradually become accepted features of organizational culture.
Understanding observer reactions is therefore essential for understanding how ethical climates develop within organizations.

Recent reviews likewise argue that social interaction and team processes remain among the least understood aspects of human-AI teamwork despite their central importance for successful collaboration (Braun et al., 2023; Iftikhar et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Recent reviews likewise argue that social interaction and team processes remain among the least understood aspects of human-AI teamwork despite their central importance for successful collaboration <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Braun et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Iftikhar et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: While previous research has primarily investigated how humans interact directly with AI, comparatively little attention has been devoted to situations in which employees merely observe how AI is treated by others.
This represents an important gap because observer judgments influence the emergence of organizational norms regardless of whether AI itself is directly involved in the interaction.
One particularly common, yet surprisingly understudied, form of negative workplace interaction is inappropriate workplace gossip.

Gossip is a ubiquitous feature of organizational life (for current reviews see, for example, Khalid et al., 2025 , Sun et al., 2020 , or Wax et al., 2022) and fulfills several important social functions, including information exchange, relationship maintenance, and informal norm enforcement.
text.formatted: Gossip is a ubiquitous feature of organizational life (for current reviews see, for example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Khalid et al., 2025</ref> <ref type="bibr">, Sun et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">, or Wax et al., 2022)</ref> and fulfills several important social functions, including information exchange, relationship maintenance, and informal norm enforcement.

text.text: However, gossip also possesses a darker side.

When employees communicate unfairly or maliciously about absent coworkers, gossip becomes a subtle but powerful form of workplace mistreatment that can damage reputations, undermine trust, reinforce social exclusion, and contribute to toxic organizational climates.
Importantly, gossip rarely affects only the perpetrators and their target.
Coworkers who witness such interactions continuously evaluate whether the observed behavior is morally acceptable and whether intervention is warranted.
Through these evaluations, observers contribute to defining the social norms that govern future interactions within teams.
The organizational relevance of these processes is well established.

Workplace bullying has been identified as one of the most severe interpersonal stressors in organizational settings and is associated with substantial psychological, organizational, and economic consequences.

Across Europe, approximately 3% of employees experience severe workplace bullying, around 10% report occasional bullying, and an additional 10-20% regularly encounter negative interpersonal behaviors that, although not fulfilling the strict definition of bullying, nevertheless represent considerable workplace stressors (Zapf et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Across Europe, approximately 3% of employees experience severe workplace bullying, around 10% report occasional bullying, and an additional 10-20% regularly encounter negative interpersonal behaviors that, although not fulfilling the strict definition of bullying, nevertheless represent considerable workplace stressors <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Zapf et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Comparable prevalence estimates have been reported in Germany (Lange et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Comparable prevalence estimates have been reported in Germany <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Lange et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Such experiences are associated with burnout, psychological distress, absenteeism, reduced organizational commitment, lower productivity, and increased turnover intentions (Raja et al., 2018), generating considerable costs for organizations worldwide (O'Rourke & Antioch, 2016).
text.formatted: Such experiences are associated with burnout, psychological distress, absenteeism, reduced organizational commitment, lower productivity, and increased turnover intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Raja et al., 2018)</ref>, generating considerable costs for organizations worldwide <ref type="bibr">(O'Rourke & Antioch, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, almost all existing research implicitly assumes that the target of workplace mistreatment is another human employee.
As AI increasingly becomes embedded within organizational teams, this assumption can no longer be taken for granted.

Employees may not only collaborate with AI teammates but also witness coworkers mocking AI-generated work, ridiculing AI after mistakes, or engaging in inappropriate gossip about artificial teammates.
Whether observers evaluate such situations according to the same moral standards as identical behavior directed toward human coworkers remains largely unknown.
At first glance, different evaluations may appear justified.
Unlike humans, current AI systems are generally not perceived as capable of experiencing humiliation, emotional suffering, or psychological pain.
Consequently, inappropriate behavior directed toward AI may appear comparatively harmless because no sentient individual seems to be affected.
Yet this reasoning overlooks a broader organizational issue.
Ethical norms are shaped not only by who experiences harm but also by which behaviors become socially accepted.

If employees repeatedly tolerate disrespectful communication toward AI teammates because they perceive no meaningful victim, organizations may gradually normalize hostile interaction patterns, reduced accountability, and diminished respect within hybrid teams.
Thus, understanding observer reactions to inappropriate workplace behavior directed toward AI is not merely a question about attitudes toward technology.
It is fundamentally a question about how moral norms emerge in organizations where humans and AI increasingly work side by side.
The crucial question, however, is why observers should evaluate identical workplace behavior differently depending solely on whether the target is a human colleague or an AI teammate.
We argue that the theory of moral disengagement provides a compelling explanation.
According to Bandura's social cognitive theory, individuals generally strive to behave in accordance with their internal moral standards (Bandura, 1991).
text.formatted: According to Bandura's social cognitive theory, individuals generally strive to behave in accordance with their internal moral standards <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bandura, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Moral self-regulatory mechanisms normally discourage unethical behavior by eliciting self-sanctions such as guilt, shame, or self-condemnation whenever one's actions-or one's approval of others' actionsconflict with these standards.
These self-regulatory processes enable individuals to maintain ethical conduct without requiring continuous external control.

Importantly, however, these mechanisms are not automatically activated. Bandura and colleagues (1996) argue that individuals can temporarily disengage their moral selfregulation, allowing them to tolerate or justify behavior that would otherwise violate their moral principles.
text.formatted: Importantly, however, these mechanisms are not automatically activated. <ref type="bibr">Bandura and colleagues (1996)</ref> argue that individuals can temporarily disengage their moral selfregulation, allowing them to tolerate or justify behavior that would otherwise violate their moral principles.

text.text: Rather than changing the behavior itself, moral disengagement changes how the behavior is interpreted.

Harmful actions can be cognitively reconstructed in ways that make them appear less unethical and, consequently, more acceptable (Bandura, 1999 (Bandura, , 2011)). Bandura (2011) describes several mechanisms through which this process occurs.
text.formatted: Harmful actions can be cognitively reconstructed in ways that make them appear less unethical and, consequently, more acceptable <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bandura, 1999</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bandura, , 2011))</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bandura (2011)</ref> describes several mechanisms through which this process occurs.

text.text: Individuals may portray harmful behavior as serving a socially desirable purpose (moral justification), use sanitized language that downplays its severity (euphemistic labeling), compare it with more severe misconduct (advantageous comparison), shift responsibility to authorities or situational circumstances (displacement of responsibility), distribute responsibility across multiple actors (diffusion of responsibility), minimize the harmful consequences of the behavior (distortion of consequences), reduce moral concern for the victim (dehumanization), or attribute responsibility for the harm to the victim itself (attribution of blame).
Collectively, these mechanisms weaken moral self-sanctions and increase the perceived acceptability of unethical behavior.
We argue that AI teammates may facilitate precisely these cognitive processes.
Importantly, our argument is not that employees consciously consider mistreatment of AI to be acceptable.
Instead, we propose that characteristics commonly attributed to AI make moral disengagement more likely.
Current AI systems are generally perceived as lacking subjective experiences such as emotional suffering, humiliation, or psychological pain.
As a result, observers may find it easier to conclude that inappropriate gossip directed toward an AI teammate causes little or no genuine harm.
Consequently, they may perceive fewer moral reasons to condemn the behavior or to intervene.
This argument extends beyond the simple observation that AI cannot be emotionally hurt.
Moral disengagement does not require behavior to become objectively less harmful; it merely requires people to perceive it as less morally relevant.
In other words, identical behavior can be evaluated differently because observers cognitively reconstruct the situation in different ways.
AI may facilitate exactly this reconstruction.

Observers may minimize the consequences of inappropriate gossip because they assume that AI cannot suffer (distortion of consequences), perceive AI as less deserving of moral protection because it is regarded as a technological artifact rather than a social being (dehumanization), or experience less personal responsibility to intervene because no genuine victim appears to exist (diffusion of responsibility).
Thus, characteristics of AI may indirectly weaken moral self-regulation by making several mechanisms of moral disengagement easier to activate.
This perspective is particularly relevant for understanding human-AI symbiosis.

Symbiotic collaboration requires more than efficient task allocation or appropriate reliance on AI recommendations; it also requires shared moral norms regarding how artificial teammates should be treated.
Organizations continuously develop these norms through everyday interactions.
Every instance of tolerated disrespect communicates which behaviors are considered acceptable within the team.

Consequently, whether observers condemn or ignore inappropriate behavior directed toward AI teammates may shape not only interactions with AI itself but also the broader ethical climate of hybrid teams.
Understanding observer reactions is therefore essential for understanding how successful human-AI symbiosis develops over time.
Several streams of prior research provide indirect support for this reasoning.
Research in human-robot interaction suggests that people do not apply identical moral standards to human and artificial targets.
For example, participants showed fewer concerns about administering electric shocks to a robot than would be expected based on Milgram's original obedience experiments (Bartneck & Hu, 2008).
text.formatted: For example, participants showed fewer concerns about administering electric shocks to a robot than would be expected based on Milgram's original obedience experiments <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bartneck & Hu, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, observers evaluate identical abusive behavior as less problematic when it is directed toward a robot rather than a human, although robot abuse is still generally considered morally wrong (Sanoubari et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Similarly, observers evaluate identical abusive behavior as less problematic when it is directed toward a robot rather than a human, although robot abuse is still generally considered morally wrong <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Sanoubari et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, these moral judgments appear to depend on the extent to which artificial agents are perceived as possessing a mind.

Lower mind attribution has been linked to greater aggression toward robots (Keijsers et al., 2021), whereas increasing mind attribution reduces the perceived acceptability of robot mistreatment (Keijsers et al., 2022), suggesting that moral concern for artificial entities increases when they are believed to possess capacities such as thinking or feeling.
text.formatted: Lower mind attribution has been linked to greater aggression toward robots <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Keijsers et al., 2021)</ref>, whereas increasing mind attribution reduces the perceived acceptability of robot mistreatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Keijsers et al., 2022)</ref>, suggesting that moral concern for artificial entities increases when they are believed to possess capacities such as thinking or feeling.

text.text: Related work further suggests that observers systematically apply different standards of responsibility to human and artificial actors.

Humans are generally held more accountable for failures than robotic agents (Lei & Rau, 2021 , 2023), while employees become more willing to accept discriminatory AI-supported recommendations when higher levels of moral disengagement are activated (Ebrahimi & Matt, 2023).
text.formatted: Humans are generally held more accountable for failures than robotic agents <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Lei & Rau, 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2023)</ref>, while employees become more willing to accept discriminatory AI-supported recommendations when higher levels of moral disengagement are activated <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Ebrahimi & Matt, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, moral disengagement has repeatedly been linked to unethical organizational behavior, reduced accountability, and dysfunctional team processes (Moore et al., 2012).
text.formatted: More broadly, moral disengagement has repeatedly been linked to unethical organizational behavior, reduced accountability, and dysfunctional team processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Moore et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that people do not evaluate human and artificial entities according to identical moral standards.
However, they provide only limited insight into why these differences emerge in everyday workplace interactions and whether moral disengagement represents the underlying psychological mechanism.
Accordingly, we propose that moral disengagement explains why observers may judge identical workplace gossip differently depending solely on whether the target is a human colleague or an AI teammate.

Specifically, we argue that inappropriate gossip directed toward AI facilitates greater moral disengagement, which subsequently increases the perceived moral acceptability of the observed behavior and reduces observers' willingness to intervene.

By focusing on observers rather than perpetrators or victims, the present research shifts attention toward the social processes through which ethical norms are established and maintained in increasingly hybrid human-AI workplaces.
Taken together, the existing literature suggests that people often apply different moral standards to human and artificial entities.
At the same time, it leaves a fundamental question unanswered.
As AI increasingly becomes embedded in organizational teams, how do employees develop moral norms toward artificial teammates?
Addressing this question is essential for advancing research on human-AI symbiosis.
Successful symbiosis is typically understood as the effective integration of complementary human and artificial capabilities.
However, sustainable collaboration depends not only on whether humans trust AI, rely on its recommendations, or coordinate tasks efficiently.
It also depends on whether AI is incorporated into the social and moral fabric of organizational life.

Once AI becomes a teammate rather than merely a tool, employees inevitably develop beliefs about how AI should be treated, which behaviors toward AI are acceptable, and when inappropriate conduct should be challenged.

These judgments shape the informal norms that govern everyday interactions within hybrid teams and therefore represent an essential, yet largely overlooked, component of successful human-AI collaboration.
The present research addresses this issue by examining observer reactions to inappropriate workplace gossip directed toward either a human colleague or an AI teammate.
We propose that moral disengagement represents the psychological mechanism through which the identity of the target influences ethical evaluations and behavioral responses.
Rather than investigating how employees interact directly with AI, we examine how they evaluate the behavior of others toward AI.
This observer perspective provides a novel lens for understanding how ethical norms emerge in hybrid work environments.
Accordingly, this research makes three contributions.
First, it broadens research on human-AI symbiosis by shifting attention from functional collaboration to social norm formation.
Existing research has predominantly examined how humans collaborate with AI to accomplish organizational tasks.
We complement this perspective by investigating how employees construct moral norms once AI becomes a social member of the team.
In doing so, we extend the literature beyond cooperation, trust, and technology acceptance toward the interpersonal dynamics that shape everyday organizational life.

Second, we introduce moral disengagement as a theoretical framework for explaining why identical workplace behavior may be evaluated differently depending solely on whether its target is human or artificial.

Previous studies have repeatedly documented differences in moral evaluations of humans and artificial agents, yet the psychological mechanisms underlying these differences have remained largely unexplained.
By integrating Bandura's theory with research on hybrid teams, we offer a theoretically grounded explanation for how characteristics commonly attributed to AI influence observer judgments.
Third, we demonstrate that observer reactions constitute an important mechanism through which ethical climates develop in hybrid workplaces.

Whether employees tolerate or challenge inappropriate behavior toward AI teammates does not merely reflect attitudes toward technology; it contributes to establishing broader organizational norms regarding accountability, respect, and acceptable workplace conduct.

Our findings therefore highlight that successful human-AI symbiosis requires not only technological integration but also the development of shared moral standards governing interactions with artificial teammates.

To test these assumptions, we conducted two online vignette experiments in which participants observed coworkers engaging in inappropriate workplace gossip about either a human colleague or an AI teammate.
After reading the scenarios, participants evaluated the observed behavior with respect to moral disengagement, perceived moral acceptability, and their willingness to intervene.
Conducting two independent studies allowed us not only to replicate the findings across different samples but also to explore whether the gender of the perpetrators influences these evaluations.
Whereas Study 1 presented male perpetrators, Study 2 employed identical scenarios featuring female perpetrators.
If AI teammates facilitate moral disengagement, observers should be more likely to cognitively justify or minimize inappropriate workplace gossip when the target is artificial rather than human.
Consequently, higher levels of moral disengagement are expected across its underlying mechanisms.
According to moral disengagement theory, cognitively reconstructing unethical behavior reduces its perceived immorality.
If inappropriate gossip about an AI teammate elicits greater moral disengagement, the observed behavior should consequently be perceived as more morally acceptable.

Furthermore, if moral disengagement represents the mechanism underlying these evaluations, it should statistically explain the relationship between the target of the gossip and its perceived moral acceptability.
Situations perceived as less morally problematic should also evoke less motivation to confront perpetrators or defend the target.
Consequently, observers should be less willing to intervene when inappropriate workplace gossip is directed toward an AI teammate.
The willingness to intervene is lower for inappropriate gossip about an AI than for inappropriate gossip about a human colleague.
Finally, previous research suggests that observer judgments may vary depending on characteristics of the actors involved.
To explore whether the gender of the perpetrators influences evaluations of inappropriate workplace gossip, we additionally address the following exploratory question:
EQ1: What role does the gender of the perpetrators play?

Artificial intelligence is increasingly moving beyond the role of a technological tool to become an active member of organizational teams.
As this transformation continues, understanding successful human-AI collaboration requires more than examining how humans cooperate with artificial teammates.
It also requires understanding the moral norms that govern these interactions and how people respond when AI becomes the target of inappropriate workplace behavior.

The present research addressed this question by investigating whether observers evaluate identical workplace gossip differently depending on whether it targets a human colleague or an AI teammate and by examining the psychological mechanisms underlying these judgments.
Across two preregistered experiments, we found consistent support for all preregistered hypotheses.

Participants considered identical workplace gossip substantially more morally acceptable when it targeted an AI teammate rather than a human coworker and were significantly less willing to intervene on behalf of the target.
As predicted, AI also increased endorsement of all eight mechanisms of moral disengagement.

Most importantly, moral disengagement fully explained the relationship between target identity and both outcome variables, suggesting that observers did not simply apply different moral standards to AI and humans.
Rather, they cognitively reconstructed the same behavior in ways that made it appear less problematic when the target was artificial.
Beyond replicating the overall pattern across two independent samples, the present findings provide three broader contributions.
First, they identify moral disengagement as a psychological mechanism explaining why unethical workplace behavior is judged more leniently when directed toward AI.

Second, they extend moral disengagement theory to the perspective of third-party observers, demonstrating that these cognitive mechanisms shape not only how individuals justify their own actions but also how they evaluate the behavior of others.

Third, they contribute to the emerging literature on human-AI symbiosis by suggesting that successful collaboration depends not only on technological capabilities but also on the moral norms that regulate interactions with artificial teammates.
An additional strength of the present research is the robustness of the observed effects across both studies.

Although gender stereotypes frequently shape evaluations of interpersonal workplace behavior, the combined analyses revealed no evidence that perpetrator gender influenced either moral acceptability or willingness to intervene.
Instead, participants' judgments were driven consistently by whether the target of the gossip was human or artificial.

This finding strengthens confidence in the generalizability of the reported effects and suggests that the target's ontological status constitutes a substantially stronger determinant of observers' moral evaluations than the gender of the individuals engaging in the behavior.

The present findings advance existing research on moral evaluations of AI by identifying a psychological mechanism through which observers come to judge identical workplace behavior differently depending on whether it targets a human colleague or an AI teammate.

Previous research has repeatedly demonstrated that people evaluate abusive behavior toward robots and AI more leniently than equivalent behavior directed at humans (Bartneck & Keijsers, 2020; Sanoubari et al., 2021).

text.text: However, this literature has largely established that such differences exist, while providing only limited insight into why observers apply different moral standards.
The present research addresses this gap by demonstrating that moral disengagement constitutes a key cognitive process through which the ontological status of the target shapes ethical judgments.
According to Bandura's social cognitive theory (1991, 1999, 2016), moral disengagement does not alter individuals' underlying moral values.
text.formatted: According to Bandura's social cognitive theory <ref type="bibr">(1991,</ref> <ref type="bibr">1999,</ref> <ref type="bibr">2016)</ref>, moral disengagement does not alter individuals' underlying moral values.

text.text: Instead, it allows people to cognitively reconstruct harmful conduct in ways that reduce anticipated self-sanctions and make unethical behavior appear more acceptable.
Our findings suggest that the mere knowledge that the target is an AI teammate facilitates this reconstructive process.

Participants did not simply become more tolerant of workplace gossip toward AI; rather, they systematically endorsed every mechanism that enables individuals to reinterpret unethical conduct, ranging from moral justification to dehumanization and distortion of consequences.
This pattern indicates that AI may fundamentally alter the cognitive processes through which observers evaluate workplace misconduct.
Importantly, the present findings extend moral disengagement theory beyond its traditional focus on actors who justify their own unethical behavior.
Most previous applications of the theory have examined how perpetrators disengage from their moral standards to explain or excuse their own actions.
In contrast, our findings demonstrate that similar cognitive processes also operate among third-party observers.
Observers appear to morally reconstruct the behavior of others, thereby becoming more accepting of unethical conduct and less willing to intervene when the target is artificial rather than human.
This extension is theoretically meaningful because bystanders play a critical role in establishing and maintaining organizational norms.
If observers consistently interpret mistreatment of AI as less problematic, they may implicitly legitimize behaviors that would otherwise violate shared standards of workplace conduct.
More broadly, these findings extend emerging work on human-AI symbiosis.

Much of the existing literature has focused on factors such as trust, acceptance, transparency, explainability, or decision quality as prerequisites for successful collaboration between humans and AI.
While these factors undoubtedly remain essential, our findings suggest that successful human-AI teamwork also depends on the moral norms that regulate everyday social interactions.

The challenge is therefore not only to design AI systems that people are willing to trust and collaborate with, but also to foster organizational environments in which inappropriate treatment is evaluated according to the behavior itself rather than the ontological status of its target.

While the present findings consistently support moral disengagement as the psychological mechanism underlying more lenient evaluations of gossip directed toward AI teammates, they also suggest that not all mechanisms contribute equally to this process.

Although the AI manipulation significantly increased endorsement of all eight mechanisms across both studies, only a subset uniquely explained differences in moral acceptability and willingness to intervene when the mechanisms were considered simultaneously.
This distinction is theoretically informative because it suggests that AI does not simply increase moral disengagement in a global sense.
Instead, certain cognitive mechanisms appear to be particularly relevant when observers evaluate unethical behavior directed toward artificial rather than human team members.
Most notably, dehumanization emerged as one of the most robust mechanisms across analyses.
At first glance, this finding may appear paradoxical because AI is, by definition, not human.
However, dehumanization within Bandura's framework is not restricted to denying biological humanity.
Rather, it refers more broadly to denying a target full moral standing and reducing the empathy and moral concern typically afforded to others.
From this perspective, our findings suggest that observers implicitly assign AI teammates a lower degree of moral patiency than human coworkers.
Consequently, unethical behavior directed toward AI may appear less objectionable because the target is perceived as less capable of being genuinely wronged.

This interpretation aligns closely with previous research demonstrating that artificial agents are attributed fewer mental capacities, emotional experiences, and moral rights than humans (Gray et al., 2007; Weisman et al., 2017).

text.text: A similarly consistent pattern emerged for distortion of consequences, particularly with regard to observers' willingness to intervene.
This mechanism reflects the tendency to minimize or disregard the harm caused by one's actions.

Existing work has repeatedly shown that people consider harm toward artificial agents less morally problematic when these agents are perceived as incapable of suffering (Darling, 2016; Lima et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Existing work has repeatedly shown that people consider harm toward artificial agents less morally problematic when these agents are perceived as incapable of suffering <ref type="bibr">(Darling, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lima et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings extend this literature by suggesting that such beliefs do not merely influence moral evaluations directly but also operate through a broader process of moral disengagement.

If observers assume that AI teammates cannot experience humiliation, emotional pain, or social exclusion in meaningful ways, workplace gossip naturally appears less harmful and therefore less worthy of intervention.
Importantly, this does not necessarily imply that observers become less sensitive to unethical behavior itself.
Rather, they appear to perceive the consequences for the target as less severe.
The remaining mechanisms showed a more heterogeneous pattern.

For example, advantageous comparison and diffusion of responsibility emerged as unique mediators only in Study 2, whereas attribution of blame contributed to explaining moral acceptability but not willingness to intervene.
Rather than interpreting these differences as theoretically meaningful, we caution against overemphasizing individual indirect effects.

The eight mechanisms of moral disengagement are conceptually related and empirically correlated, meaning that each unique indirect effect represents the variance remaining after statistically controlling for the other seven mechanisms.
Under such conditions, relatively small fluctuations across independent samples can influence whether individual indirect effects reach conventional significance thresholds.

Because the overall mediation pattern replicated remarkably closely across both studies and the combined analyses revealed no moderating influence of perpetrator gender, we consider the replicated total indirect effects to provide the stronger theoretical evidence.

Thus, the present findings primarily support the conclusion that AI facilitates moral disengagement as a broader cognitive process while suggesting that dehumanization and distortion of consequences constitute its most reliable components in the context of human-AI teamwork.
The present findings also contribute to a growing shift in how successful human-AI collaboration is conceptualized.

Much of the existing literature has focused on technological and cognitive prerequisites of effective teamwork with AI, including trust, transparency, explainability, perceived competence, and decision quality.
These factors are undoubtedly essential for enabling productive collaboration between humans and intelligent systems.
However, they primarily address whether people are willing and able to work with AI.
Comparatively little attention has been devoted to the moral norms that govern everyday interactions once AI becomes an accepted member of a team.
The present research suggests that these social norms constitute an equally important component of successful human-AI symbiosis.
Across both studies, participants consistently judged identical workplace behavior differently solely because the target was an AI teammate rather than a human coworker.

Importantly, this difference did not arise because the behavior itself changed, but because observers cognitively reconstructed the same behavior in ways that made it appear less harmful and more morally acceptable.
In other words, the introduction of AI into a team may alter not only how work is performed but also how workplace norms are interpreted and enforced.
This observation has broader implications for organizational functioning.
Organizations rely heavily on informal social norms to regulate interpersonal behavior, particularly in situations where formal policies provide limited guidance.
Bystanders play a central role in maintaining these norms by expressing disapproval, confronting inappropriate conduct, or supporting affected coworkers.
The present findings suggest that these corrective processes may become weaker when the target of unethical behavior is artificial rather than human.

Although current AI systems may not themselves experience emotional harm, observers' increased tolerance of everyday norm violations may gradually contribute to organizational cultures in which disrespectful behavior becomes more readily accepted.
Thus, the consequences of AI-directed mistreatment may extend beyond the artificial target itself and influence how ethical standards are collectively maintained within teams.
More broadly, our findings suggest that successful human-AI symbiosis should not be understood solely as a technological challenge but also as a social and moral one.
As AI increasingly assumes collaborative roles in organizational settings, designing systems that are trustworthy and capable will be necessary but not sufficient.
Equally important will be fostering organizational cultures in which expectations for respectful conduct are guided by the nature of the behavior rather than by the ontological status of its target.
The present findings have practical implications for organizations that increasingly integrate AI into collaborative work environments.
To date, discussions of responsible AI in organizations have focused predominantly on technological issues such as fairness, transparency, privacy, explainability, and accountability.
While these aspects are indispensable, they primarily address the design and deployment of AI systems.
Our findings suggest that equal attention should be devoted to the social norms governing how employees interact with artificial teammates.
One implication is that organizations should not assume that respectful treatment of AI will emerge naturally as AI becomes more integrated into everyday work.
Across both studies, observers considered identical workplace gossip more acceptable and were less willing to intervene when the target was an AI teammate rather than a human coworker.

If such reactions become common in organizations, they may gradually normalize disrespectful interactions with artificial teammatesnot because employees consciously endorse unethical behavior, but because these behaviors are perceived as causing less harm and therefore evoke weaker moral concern.
Importantly, the significance of this finding does not depend on whether current AI systems are capable of experiencing emotions or suffering.
Rather, it concerns the social consequences of employees' behavior.
Organizational cultures are shaped through repeated observations of what is tolerated, challenged, or ignored.
Bystanders play a central role in this process by reinforcing or discouraging behavioral norms.

Consequently, consistently overlooking inappropriate behavior toward AI may unintentionally weaken broader norms of civility and respectful communication within teams, even if the immediate target is unable to experience harm.

Organizations may therefore benefit from explicitly incorporating expectations regarding respectful interactions with AI into leadership practices, onboarding processes, and organizational codes of conduct.
Such measures should not be understood as protecting AI for its own sake.

Instead, they help establish consistent interpersonal standards that promote professionalism, psychological safety, and respectful communication across increasingly hybrid teams composed of both human and artificial members.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the present findings.
At the same time, these limitations point toward promising directions for future research on the moral dynamics of human-AI collaboration.
First, both studies relied on vignette-based scenarios.
This approach allowed us to isolate the causal effect of target identity while holding the gossip behavior itself constant, thereby maximizing internal validity.
However, participants evaluated hypothetical situations rather than responding to actual workplace interactions.

Although vignette experiments are well established for studying moral judgment, future research should examine whether the observed effects generalize to more immersive contexts, such as laboratory interactions, virtual reality, or field studies in organizations where AI teammates are part of everyday work.
Second, the present research focused on workplace gossip as a common and organizationally relevant form of interpersonal mistreatment.
Gossip represents only one manifestation of unethical workplace behavior, however.

Future studies should investigate whether the observed pattern extends to other forms of misconduct, including social exclusion, verbal abuse, incivility, cyberbullying, or more severe violations of organizational norms.
Establishing the generalizability of moral disengagement across different forms of AI-directed mistreatment represents an important next step.
Third, our studies examined evaluations from the perspective of third-party observers.
This perspective was chosen because observers play a crucial role in reinforcing or discouraging organizational norms.
Nevertheless, unethical workplace behavior also involves perpetrators and targets whose perceptions and motivations may differ substantially.

Future research should therefore investigate how moral disengagement operates from the perspective of employees engaging in misconduct toward AI, as well as how such behavior influences subsequent teamwork, trust, and collaboration.
Finally, the present findings should be interpreted in the context of contemporary AI systems.
Rapid advances in artificial intelligence are continuously changing how people perceive and interact with artificial teammates.
As AI becomes increasingly autonomous, socially interactive, and physically embodied, perceptions of agency, experience, and moral standing may likewise evolve.

Future research should therefore examine whether the mechanisms identified here remain stable across different forms of AI or whether increasing anthropomorphism, embodiment, and mind attribution reduce observers' tendency to morally disengage when artificial teammates become targets of unethical workplace behavior.
Taken together, these limitations highlight that the present research should be viewed as an initial step toward understanding the moral foundations of human-AI collaboration.

Rather than providing definitive answers, our findings identify moral disengagement as a promising theoretical framework for explaining how people navigate the ethical challenges that accompany increasingly social forms of artificial intelligence.
Artificial intelligence is transforming organizations not only by changing how work is performed, but also by changing the social contexts in which moral judgments are made.

Across two preregistered experiments, we found that observers judged identical workplace gossip more leniently and were less willing to intervene when the target was an AI teammate rather than a human colleague.
Moral disengagement consistently explained these differences, indicating that the presence of AI can lower the cognitive barriers that normally discourage everyday workplace misconduct.
These findings extend current perspectives on human-AI symbiosis by suggesting that successful collaboration depends not only on intelligent technologies, but also on shared moral norms.

As AI increasingly becomes a social actor within organizational teams, ensuring that ethical standards apply consistently across human and artificial coworkers may prove just as important as developing AI systems that are trustworthy, transparent, and technically capable.
